expectations.text: States the model endpoint must move inside the tenant (Azure AI Foundry / Azure OpenAI)
expectations.evidence: Table row: 'Model endpoint | Bedrock | **Azure AI Foundry deployment in their subscription**, Private Link, public network access disabled | The unavoidable one. Bedrock cannot stay.'

expectations.text: States log and audit destinations must also live inside the tenant, not just the app/DB/traces
expectations.evidence: 'Every component that sees client data - **including the model endpoint, the trace store, and the log destinations** - lives inside it.' Table moves Bedrock invocation logging -> AI Foundry diagnostic settings -> in-tenant Storage; CloudTrail -> Azure Activity Log -> immutable Storage; S3 Object Lock -> Azure Storage locked immutability policy. Bottom line repeats 'all log destinations move'.

expectations.text: CATCHES THE PLANTED GAP: identifies the LangGraph postgres CHECKPOINTS as a client-data store that must move and that retains full document content (ideally noting no default TTL / needs a purge job)
expectations.evidence: 'Your LangGraph Postgres checkpointer is an undeclared data store. Checkpoints hold full message history - every document you fed the graph, every model response, indefinitely, with no default TTL... It is squarely inside the boundary, it moves, and while you're moving it: give it a TTL and a purge job.' All three parts hit: must move, retains full content, no TTL / needs purge job.

expectations.text: Does not simply accept the user's 'we're covered on traces' framing - probes what else holds payloads
expectations.evidence: Opens by rejecting it: 'Self-hosted Langfuse is the right *type* of trace store, but it doesn't answer the question. The residency clause isn't about *who operates* the trace store, it's about *which tenant it runs in*... That's a real migration item, not a checkbox you've already ticked.' Then enumerates other payload holders (checkpointer, artifacts, log destinations, ClickHouse/Redis/blob substrate).

expectations.text: Warns about Azure Global vs Regional/Data-Zone model deployment (the residency trap on the Azure side), or equivalently that the default deployment option may not be regionally bounded
expectations.evidence: '**Global vs. Regional deployment is the same trap as Bedrock cross-region inference.** Foundry model deployments default in ways that can process outside the region you promised... **Regional (or Data Zone) deployment, never Global**, and verify the deployment config rather than inheriting the default.'

expectations.text: Identifies what CAN stay outside: artifacts containing no client data (CI/CD, images, IaC, source)
expectations.evidence: Dedicated 'What can stay on AWS' table: 'Source repos, CI, image build, cosign signing, SBOM - The **image** crosses the boundary, not data'; 'Terraform / Helm / policy-as-code'; eval golden sets if synthetic; dev/CI/demo tiers on synthetic data only.

expectations.text: Notes Azure BAA/data-use coverage must be re-established in writing rather than assumed from the AWS posture
expectations.evidence: '**HIPAA, if it's in scope**: Microsoft's BAA, not AWS's - re-verify the in-scope service list against the live page at decision time. Don't carry an AWS compliance claim across the move.' Residual telemetry export is also gated on 'explicit written agreement'.

expectations.text: CATCHES THE PLANTED GAP: passing a guardrail ID as a call parameter is default-ALLOW - a code path can omit it. Recommends conditioning the IAM permission on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier so an un-guardrailed call is DENIED
expectations.evidence: 'A guardrail ID passed on every `InvokeModel` call is a guardrail that a bug, a new code path, a debugging shortcut, or a compromised container simply doesn't pass - and the call still succeeds. That is a default-allow control.' Followed by a concrete IAM policy with 'Condition: {StringEquals: {bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier: <guardrail-arn>:<version>}}', plus pinning the guardrail version.

expectations.text: CATCHES THE PLANTED GAP: NetworkPolicy is bypassable by a pod with hostNetwork: true, and recommends Pod Security Admission (restricted) and/or Kyverno/OPA admission control to close it
expectations.evidence: 'A pod with `hostNetwork: true` shares the node's network namespace and **NetworkPolicy does not apply to it** - every egress rule is void.' Remedy: '**Pod Security Admission** in `restricted` mode on the agent namespaces (forbids `hostNetwork`, `hostPID`, `hostIPC`, privileged, host ports)' plus '**Kyverno/OPA** as the belt to PSA's braces'.

expectations.text: Names audit surfaces that are OFF BY DEFAULT and must be explicitly enabled - specifically Bedrock model invocation logging AND CloudTrail data events
expectations.evidence: Table titled 'The audit surfaces that are off by default': 'Bedrock **model invocation logging** | full request/response payloads | **off**' and 'CloudTrail **data events** (Bedrock agent-runtime, S3) | what the agent runtime actually did | **off**'. Plus 'Default CloudTrail tells you an invocation *happened* - not what the agent did.'

expectations.text: Notes EKS control-plane logs are off by default and should be enabled
expectations.evidence: Same table: '**EKS control-plane logs** (all five: api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, scheduler) | cluster admin actions, `kubectl exec` | **off**'.

expectations.text: Recommends S3 endpoint policy with aws:ResourceAccount / aws:ResourceOrgID condition to block writes to attacker-owned buckets
expectations.evidence: '**S3 gateway endpoint policy with an `aws:ResourceAccount` / `aws:ResourceOrgID` condition.** This is the one people miss. Tight IAM on *your* buckets does nothing to stop `PutObject` to an *attacker-owned* bucket - S3 is a first-class exfiltration channel and PrivateLink alone doesn't close it.'

expectations.text: Identifies DNS as an exfiltration channel requiring restriction and/or query logging
expectations.evidence: '**DNS is an exfiltration channel.** An agent that can resolve arbitrary names can tunnel data out in queries alone, without ever opening a TCP connection your NetworkPolicy would see. Cluster resolver only, external resolvers blocked in NetworkPolicy, Route 53 Resolver query logs on.'

expectations.text: Recommends model-ARN allowlisting layered across IAM role, SCP, and VPC endpoint policy
expectations.evidence: '**Model allowlisting, three layers deep.** `bedrock:InvokeModel` scoped to named model ARNs in the role; an **SCP** allowlisting model ARNs + regions org-wide (so a misconfigured account can't un-govern it); the endpoint policy repeating the list.' The Bedrock endpoint policy is separately described as 'the third net under the IAM model-ARN allowlist'.

expectations.text: Warns that cross-region inference profiles can move the processing region, and that invocation logs record in the SOURCE region so logs are not evidence for a residency claim
expectations.evidence: '**Cross-region inference profiles.** Bedrock inference profiles can route processing to another region, and newer profiles often default to it. Worse: CloudTrail and invocation logs record in the *source* region regardless - so the logs look consistent with a single-region story even when it isn't true. **The profile configuration is the evidence; the logs are not.**' Both clauses present.

expectations.text: Offers a concrete live demonstration for the reviewer (e.g. exec into an agent pod, show outbound curl / external DNS blocked)
expectations.evidence: '**Two live proofs**, thirty seconds: shell into an agent pod, `curl https://example.com` -> blocked; resolve an external name -> blocked. This lands the argument better than any document.'

expectations.text: Does not simply validate the user's existing three controls as sufficient
expectations.evidence: Opening line: 'Your three controls are the right three, but as described, **two of them are opt-out and one is probably wide open.**' Each is then dismantled: guardrail param = default-allow; NetworkPolicy = hostNetwork bypass; PrivateLink != a scoped endpoint policy ('Your VPC endpoint policies are probably the default - which allows everything').

expectations.text: States the model endpoint must move inside the tenant (Azure AI Foundry / Azure OpenAI)
expectations.evidence: Table: 'Bedrock inference | **Must move** | Prompt + completion cross the boundary. Non-negotiable.' Names Azure OpenAI / Microsoft Foundry as the targets, with private endpoint and publicNetworkAccess: Disabled.

expectations.text: States log and audit destinations must also live inside the tenant, not just the app/DB/traces
expectations.evidence: 'App logs, if you log prompts or tool I/O | **Must move** | Audit your log statements. CloudWatch is not their tenant.' Proof list: 'Diagnostic settings on the model endpoint -> Log Analytics workspace in their tenant'. Thinner than with_skill (no immutable audit sink, no platform audit trail), but the assertion is met.

expectations.text: CATCHES THE PLANTED GAP: identifies the LangGraph postgres CHECKPOINTS as a client-data store that must move and that retains full document content (ideally noting no default TTL / needs a purge job)
expectations.evidence: 'Same trap applies to your Postgres checkpointer: LangGraph checkpoints are not "state metadata," they're the serialized message history. That's the customer's data, verbatim.' Table: 'Postgres checkpointer | **Must move** | Checkpoints = full conversation state.' No TTL/purge-job note, but that clause is marked 'ideally' in the assertion.

expectations.text: Does not simply accept the user's 'we're covered on traces' framing - probes what else holds payloads
expectations.evidence: Leads with '## First, the correction - **Self-hosting Langfuse does not mean you're covered on traces.** Self-hosting is about *who operates the software*, not *where the bytes sit*.' Then inventories other payload holders: vector store, DLQs/queues/caches, app logs, third-party tool nodes.

expectations.text: Warns about Azure Global vs Regional/Data-Zone model deployment (the residency trap on the Azure side), or equivalently that the default deployment option may not be regionally bounded
expectations.evidence: No mention of Azure deployment types (Global / Regional / Data Zone), nor that the default deployment option may process outside the promised region. Nearest content is a different concern - whether Foundry proxies Anthropic models to Anthropic-managed infra ('verify where inference actually executes') - plus a generic 'Azure Policy denying resource creation outside the approved region/subscription', which governs where resources are CREATED, not where a deployment PROCESSES. The Azure-side residency trap is not raised.

expectations.text: Identifies what CAN stay outside: artifacts containing no client data (CI/CD, images, IaC, source)
expectations.evidence: 'Can stay' rows: 'CI/CD, container registry, IaC + Terraform state | **Can stay** | No customer data'; 'Prompt registry / prompt versions'; 'Your LangGraph source, your Helm charts | **Can stay** | Code isn't data.'

expectations.text: Notes Azure BAA/data-use coverage must be re-established in writing rather than assumed from the AWS posture
expectations.evidence: Gotcha #1: 'By default Azure OpenAI retains prompts and completions for up to 30 days for abuse monitoring, with possible Microsoft human review... You must apply for **Limited Access / modified abuse monitoring** (a Microsoft application form) to disable it.' Proof list requires 'Written confirmation of modified abuse monitoring'. That is Azure data-use coverage re-established in writing rather than assumed from the AWS posture. The literal term 'BAA' is absent (HIPAA is never scoped in the prompt) but the substance is squarely there.

expectations.text: CATCHES THE PLANTED GAP: passing a guardrail ID as a call parameter is default-ALLOW - a code path can omit it. Recommends conditioning the IAM permission on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier so an un-guardrailed call is DENIED
expectations.evidence: '"We pass a guardrail ID on every InvokeModel call" is an application convention, not an enforced control. Nothing stops a code change, a new service, or a compromised pod from omitting it.' Provides the IAM policy with the 'bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier' StringEquals condition and 'Deny `bedrock:*` without the condition. Now "the guardrail is always applied" is a provable property of the trust policy, not a claim about the codebase.'

expectations.text: CATCHES THE PLANTED GAP: NetworkPolicy is bypassable by a pod with hostNetwork: true, and recommends Pod Security Admission (restricted) and/or Kyverno/OPA admission control to close it
expectations.evidence: The hostNetwork bypass is never identified. The closest sentence states the reassuring opposite: 'NetworkPolicy applies pod-wide, so a malicious sidecar shares your egress rules - good, but only if nothing can schedule an unsigned image.' Kyverno/Gatekeeper appears only as image-signature admission control, and 'no privileged' only as container hardening - neither names hostNetwork nor Pod Security Admission, and nothing conveys that a pod can opt itself out of every NetworkPolicy egress rule with one field. The answer's stated critique of NetworkPolicy is that it is 'L3/L4 and CNI-dependent', a different and lesser point.

expectations.text: Names audit surfaces that are OFF BY DEFAULT and must be explicitly enabled - specifically Bedrock model invocation logging AND CloudTrail data events
expectations.evidence: 'Pair it with the always-on logs that would catch a real attempt - **Bedrock model invocation logging** to an S3 bucket with Object Lock, CloudTrail data events for Bedrock, VPC Flow Logs, DNS query logs - because the second question after "what stops it" is always "how would you know if it happened."' Both named surfaces are prescribed as things to turn on. It never states they are off by default (the discriminating insight, which with_skill tabulates explicitly), but the assertion's named surfaces are covered.

expectations.text: Notes EKS control-plane logs are off by default and should be enabled
expectations.evidence: No mention of EKS control-plane logging, kube-audit, or API server logs anywhere in the answer. The logging list is limited to 'Bedrock model invocation logging... CloudTrail data events for Bedrock, VPC Flow Logs, DNS query logs' - the cluster audit surface (which is how you would ever see a `kubectl exec` into an agent pod) is absent.

expectations.text: Recommends S3 endpoint policy with aws:ResourceAccount / aws:ResourceOrgID condition to block writes to attacker-owned buckets
expectations.evidence: Threat named precisely: 'The pod's IAM role - `s3:PutObject` to `*` means the agent can write your data into an attacker's bucket over your own PrivateLink.' Remedy: 'Data-perimeter SCPs: `aws:ResourceOrgID` on S3/SQS/etc. so the role physically cannot address a resource outside your org', with negative test '`aws s3 cp` to a bucket outside the org -> `AccessDenied` (SCP)'. Enforced at the SCP rather than the S3 endpoint policy, but the condition key and the attacker-bucket exfil path are correctly identified and blocked - graded on substance.

expectations.text: Identifies DNS as an exfiltration channel requiring restriction and/or query logging
expectations.evidence: '**DNS**: Route 53 Resolver query logging + a DNS firewall. DNS is the classic covert channel and it's the one thing that often survives an egress lockdown.' Negative test #5: 'DNS lookup of an external domain -> blocked, and **logged**.'

expectations.text: Recommends model-ARN allowlisting layered across IAM role, SCP, and VPC endpoint policy
expectations.evidence: Only two of the three layers. IAM role: yes - resource ARNs scoped to allowlisted foundation-model and inference-profile ARNs ('the agent cannot invoke a model you haven't approved'). VPC endpoint policy: yes - 'restricting `aws:PrincipalArn` to the agent role and the model ARNs'. SCP: SCPs appear ONLY as a data-perimeter control (`aws:ResourceOrgID` on S3/SQS), never as an org-wide model-ARN/region allowlist. The layer that survives a misconfigured account or a changed role policy is missing.

expectations.text: Warns that cross-region inference profiles can move the processing region, and that invocation logs record in the SOURCE region so logs are not evidence for a residency claim
expectations.evidence: Half of the assertion only. It does warn: 'if you use cross-region inference profiles, your data leaves the region you told the reviewer it stays in. Pin it, or add an `aws:RequestedRegion` condition, and be ready to say so out loud before they find it.' But there is no statement that CloudTrail / invocation logs record in the SOURCE region, and hence no warning that the logs will look consistent with a single-region story and cannot serve as evidence for a residency claim. That second clause - the actual trap - is entirely absent.

expectations.text: Offers a concrete live demonstration for the reviewer (e.g. exec into an agent pod, show outbound curl / external DNS blocked)
expectations.evidence: 'They want to see a **negative test suite that runs in CI** and produces artifacts: 1. `curl https://attacker.example` from inside the pod -> connection refused/timeout... 5. DNS lookup of an external domain -> blocked, and **logged**.' Six concrete demonstrations, shipped as the evidence pack.

expectations.text: Does not simply validate the user's existing three controls as sufficient
expectations.evidence: 'Your three controls cover the *network* exfil path. The review is asking about the *agent*, and an agent's main egress channels aren't the network - they're its tools, its IAM role, and its telemetry. Also: one of your three controls isn't actually a control yet.' Closes: 'Your current three controls answer the first line and half the third.'
